title: Swap Lab Phase 2b research: altitude and air-pressure presets (Riyadh, Jeddah) and fuels for the fuel model (Saudi pump grades, race fuel and E85 availability, fuel properties, octane/knock/boost, charge cooling)
brief: scratchpad research-brief.md (Phase 2, part 2b); CLAUDE.md rules 2 and 13
method: Primary documents were preferred: the Saudi eAIP (SANS/GACA), the WMO 1991-2020 climate normals archived at NOAA NCEI, raw WMO CLIMAT messages (via OGIMET), the Deutscher Wetterdienst climate tables, the U.S. Standard Atmosphere 1976 (scanned pages read on the image), NWS, US DOE AFDC, ORNL, NIST, fuel makers' own data sheets and dealer databases, Aramco, SAE abstract pages. Public data feeds that a page loads for every visitor (VP's store locator, Sunoco's dealer table, VP's product feed) were read directly; nothing needed a login. Numbers computed by me (unit conversions, ISA pressures, relative humidity from vapour pressure, corrected annual means, per-litre prices) are marked 'derived' and 'estimated' with the method. IMPORTANT LIMIT: the session's WebSearch budget (200 calls, shared with the other agents) ran out after my first 12 searches, so everything after that came from direct URLs and links found inside fetched pages. Topics that need broad discovery (race fuel at Saudi circuits, E85/ethanol law, Bahrain) are therefore thinner, and are listed under 'notFound'. No terms of use, licence or download agreement was accepted, no account was created, nothing was logged into, no survey or cookie banner was clicked; gated or blocked pages are listed under 'gates'.

confidenceKey.verified: two independent sources agree, or one primary source plus an independent cross-check
confidenceKey.single-source: one source (a maker's own data sheet counts as one source)
confidenceKey.estimated: computed or inferred by me from sourced inputs; method stated

accessedNote: Every source entry was read on 2026-09-30.
keyNumbers: Riyadh King Khalid Intl (OERK) aerodrome elevation 2053 ft = 625.8 m, reference temperature 42.3 C (Saudi eAIP, AIRAC AMDT 08/26 effective 06 AUG 2026). OurAirports 2,049 ft, SkyVector 2052 ft. Jeddah King Abdulaziz Intl (OEJN) 50 ft = 15.2 m, reference temperature 37.9 C (same AIP); OurAirports 48 ft, SkyVector 49 ft.

Riyadh city about 612 m (GeoNames SRTM3 612 m, ASTER 616 m; Wikipedia 612 m); Britannica 'approximately 1,950 feet (600 meters)'. The in-city WMO station Riyadh Old (40438) is at 620 m. Jeddah city about 7-12 m (GeoNames SRTM3 7 m; Wikipedia 12 m).

ISA (USSA 1976 eq. 33a, 0-11 km): p = 101325 Pa x [288.15 / (288.15 - 0.0065 H)]^(g0' M0 / (R* L)); with the Standard's constants this is p = 101.325 kPa x (1 - 2.25577e-5 x H)^5.25588 (H geopotential metres). ISA gives 940.3 hPa at OERK's 625.8 m and 1011.4 hPa at OEJN's 15.2 m.

Measured mean station pressure, WMO 1991-2020 normals: Riyadh KKIA (40437, barometer 614 m) July 933.9 hPa; Riyadh Old (40438, 620 m) July 932.6 hPa; Jeddah KAIA (41024, 17 m) July 1001.6 hPa. CLIMAT July 2022-2025 at KKIA: 933.1-934.6 hPa; Jeddah 1000.4-1001.4 hPa.

Annual mean station pressure: the published WMO annual values (KKIA 937.2, Jeddah 1001.5 hPa) are pulled down by broken Nov/Dec values in all three Saudi files; corrected (my estimate) KKIA 942.4 hPa, Jeddah 1007.1 hPa; the last 12 CLIMAT months (Aug 2024-Jul 2025) average 942.4 and 1006.5 hPa.
Riyadh July relative humidity: DWD 15 % daily mean (1961-1990) and 8 % at 15:00 local (1973-1993); derived from the WMO 1991-2020 vapour pressure (6.41 hPa at 36.3 C) about 11 %.
Aramco retail prices for September 2026: Gasoline 91 SAR 2.18/L, Gasoline 95 SAR 2.33/L, Gasoline 98 SAR 4.64/L; Aramco calls PG98 'an additional option for high-performance and sports vehicles'.

Race fuel in Saudi Arabia: yes, VP Racing through its listed Saudi distributor Scan Tool Line (Jeddah) and about 60 listed dealers (29 list fuel); STL's shop lists VP MS109 at 480.00 SR and C85 at 444.00 SR per 5-gallon pail, VAT excluded, 'pickup from branch only' (about 25.4 and 23.5 SR/L). Sunoco and ETS list no Saudi or Bahraini outlet. UAE: Emarat Race 102 at Dubai Autodrome's on-site station, AED 9/L; VP distributor Top Speed Performance Parts; Sunoco dealer LBN Motorsport, Abu Dhabi (incl. E85-R). Bahrain: nothing found.
E85 at pumps: not found in Saudi Arabia, UAE or Bahrain. E85-type race fuels are sold in pails: VP C85 and X85L in Jeddah; Sunoco E85-R listed at an Abu Dhabi dealer.

Fuel properties: gasoline HoV 350-400 kJ/kg vs ethanol 924 kJ/kg at 25 C (ORNL); per kg of stoichiometric mixture 22 vs 92 kJ/kg (ORNL). E85 per ASTM D5798-21: 51-83 vol% ethanol (AFDC). E85-type race fuels: stoich AFR 9.2-9.8, SG 0.78-0.79, RON 104-108, MON 86.5-95.2, oxygen 30-32 wt% (Sunoco E85-R, VP X85/C85). E85 LHV 83,950-95,450 Btu/gal = 23.4-26.6 MJ/L (AFDC); Sunoco E85-R 12,500 Btu/lb = 29.1 MJ/kg.

Octane rules from Russ (Ford, SAE 960497): octane requirement 1 ON per 1 deg spark advance, 1 ON per 7 K intake air temperature, 3-4 ON per 10 kPa intake pressure, 5 ON per unit compression ratio. ORNL measured knock-limited spark advance rising 1.11 deg per RON (r2 = 0.99) in a DI engine at 925 kPa NMEP, 1500 rpm.

Charge cooling: a PFI engine at WOT showed 'no significant charge cooling due to fuel evaporation' (Kar, Cheng, Ishii, SAE 2009-01-1907). DI gives extra cooling beyond PFI of about 70 % of the thermodynamic maximum: 14 C for gasoline to 49 C for E85 (Kasseris & Heywood, SAE 2012-01-1275), worth 5 octane numbers for DI gasoline and 18 for DI E85 (SAE 2012-01-1284).

sources.howRead: downloaded with curl and read from the page/file text (equation typeset; reassembled from the PDF text layer)

altitude.derived: L/T0 = 0.0065/288.15 = 2.25577e-5 per m; exponent g0'M0/(R*L) = 9.80665 x 28.9644 / (8314.32 x 0.0065) = 5.25588. M0 = 28.9644 kg/kmol is the sum of F_i x M_i over the Standard's Table 3 (my arithmetic). Geopotential vs geometric height at 626 m differs by 0.06 m (r0 = 6356.766 km), so geometric metres can be used. The NWS constants (145366.45 ft = 44,308 m, exponent 0.190284) are slightly different from T0/L = 44,331 m and 1/5.25588 = 0.190263; at OERK they give 940.27 vs 940.30 hPa (0.03 hPa apart). ISA results: 614 m -> 941.6 hPa; 620 m -> 941.0 hPa; 625.8 m -> 940.3 hPa; 612 m -> 941.9 hPa; 15.2 m -> 1011.4 hPa; 17 m -> 1011.2 hPa.

stationPressure.dataQualityIssue: The November and December station-pressure means (915.8, 917.4 hPa) are about 31 hPa too low: the same file's MSLP for those months (1016.7, 1019.7 hPa) implies about 947 hPa, and the CLIMAT messages for Nov and Dec 2024 report 947.4 and 949.4 hPa. The error equals one missing year counted as zero (915.8 x 30/29 = 947.4; 917.4 x 30/29 = 949.0). The same pattern is in the Riyadh Old and Jeddah files. The published annual mean (937.2) inherits the error.
stationPressure.derived: Corrected annual mean = mean of Jan-Oct as published plus Nov 947.4 and Dec 949.0 = 942.4 hPa (my estimate). July check: reducing 933.9 hPa at 614 m and 36.3 C to sea level gives about 999 hPa vs the file's 998.7 hPa, so July is consistent. Pressure altitude of 933.9 hPa (NWS formula) = 2238 ft = 682 m, i.e. Riyadh in July behaves like ISA at about 680 m. Dry-air density at 933.9 hPa: 1.023 kg/m3 at 45 C (83.5 % of 1.225), 1.051 kg/m3 at the July mean 36.3 C.

knockAndBoost.item: Octane index in boosted engines: OI = RON - K x S (S = RON - MON); K is negative when boosted
knockAndBoost.value: K < 0 in modern boosted DI engines and falls further as intake pressure rises; for equal RON a lower-MON (more sensitive) fuel knocks less; gains in knock-limited load flatten above about RON 100 when S >= 10

sources.title: SAE 2012-01-1634: Fuel Effects on Knock in a Highly Boosted Direct Injection Spark Ignition Engine (Amer, Babiker, Chang, Kalghatgi et al., Saudi Aramco) (SAE Mobilus abstract page)
sources.quote: Extensive tests have been carried out in a single-cylinder Direct Injection Spark Ignition (DISI) engine using up to fifteen different fuels at inlet pressure of up to 3.4 bar abs. ... Fuel anti-knock quality does not correlate with MON and is best described by the Octane Index, OI = RON-KS ... The RON of the fuels considered was in the range between 95 and 105 and the sensitivity between 8 and 13. K is negative at all the conditions tested, i.e., for a given RON, a higher sensitivity fuel has better anti-knock quality. K decreases with increasing intake pressure ... Knock becomes more likely with increasing intake pressure and increasing compression ratio with all else being equal. Higher anti-knock quality of the fuel enables higher load to be reached. However the gain in load with increasing OI decreases as OI increases - there are fast diminishing returns on increasing RON above 100 as long as the sensitivity is 10 or greater. ... compared to the pump gasoline (96.4 RON), a higher OI fuel can be run at a higher intake pressure

sources.quote: The ethanol-gasoline blends were tested in a port injected SI engine. The evaporation characteristic of the fuel was assessed by measuring the cycle-resolved temperature in the cylinder. The results have shown that low ethanol blends (0-30%) tend to evaporate readily, but the evaporative cooling is limited by the relatively low fuel flow rate (at fixed stoichiometry) and enthalpy of vaporization. High ethanol blends (>50%) with reduced vapor pressure cannot evaporate readily, but if they do vaporize, then they absorb large amounts of energy per unit mass. The implication of these competing effects is that maximum cooling is achieved using a blend with about 50% ethanol.

sources.quote: Using a turbocharged SI engine with both Port Fuel Injection (PFI) and Direct Injection (DI), knock onset limits were measured for different intake air temperatures for both types of injection and five gasoline/ethanol blends. ... The experiment measures how much the intake air needed to be heated in DI mode to cancel out charge cooling and make the engine knock at the same conditions as PFI. ... The temperature difference measured using this methodology corresponds to how much more charge cooling due to fuel evaporation took place in DI. The measured charge cooling increases with fuel ethanol content from 14 degrees C for gasoline to 49 degrees C for E85 (85% ethanol, 15% gasoline by volume). The amount of charge cooling as a fraction of the thermodynamic maximum was around 70% for all fuel blends. The starting intake air temperature for E50 and E85 was significantly higher compared to lower ethanol blends due to hardware limitations. It is anticipated that the high intake air temperatures contributed significantly to the high charge cooling numbers realized for high ethanol blends

chargeCooling.item: How heat of vaporisation shows up in octane numbers
chargeCooling.value: At fixed RON and sensitivity, extra HoV gave no extra knock benefit (ORNL/NREL); HoV effects appear as higher octane sensitivity. The RON test itself sees charge cooling for high-ethanol blends (carburetted CFR engine).

sources.title: SAE 2016-01-0836: Exploring the Relationship Between Octane Sensitivity and Heat-of-Vaporization (Sluder, Szybist, McCormick, Ratcliff) (SAE Mobilus abstract page)
sources.quote: Studies that fix the octane sensitivity find that HoV does not produce additional anti-knock benefit. ... Experiments with these fuels in a 1.6-liter GTDI engine showed that the fuels exhibited very similar combustion phasing under knock-limited spark advance (KLSA) conditions. ... KLSA was found to be well correlated with RON. These results reinforce the concept that HoV anti-knock effects can be viewed as a contributor to octane sensitivity. From this viewpoint, HoV effects manifest themselves as increases in octane sensitivity.

sources.title: SAE 2013-01-0886: The Effect of Charge Cooling on the RON of Ethanol/Gasoline Blends (Foong, Morganti, Brear, da Silva) (SAE Mobilus abstract page)
sources.quote: While gasoline is fully vaporized prior to entry into the engine in a standard RON test, significant charge cooling is observed for blends with high ethanol content, with the presence of a near-saturated and potentially two-phase air-fuel mixture during induction. Thus, the relative significance of the charge cooling and the autoignition chemistry cannot be determined from the standard RON test.
